newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu seen trying to tough out scandal.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu seen trying to tough out scandal.

text.p: Benjamin Netanyahu, a political brawler who clawed his way to the top of Israel's Likud party, is limbering up for a bare-knuckle fight over corruption charges.
"The present prime minister will stay on in the job," says Health Minister Yehoshua Matza, who is close to Netanyahu.
The 47-year-old former commando has been in office less than a year and intends to resist calls for early elections over the Bar-On influence-peddling scandal.

"He is going to try to hang on by his fingernails," said Hirsh Goodman, editor of the Jerusalem Report magazine and a fierce Netanyahu critic. "If he doesn't, it goes to elections and that's the end for him."

A prolonged struggle could save Netanyahu's career in a political culture where others have weathered even worse accusations without even thinking of resigning. But the ensuing governmental paralysis could hamper Washington's efforts to nurture withered Israeli-Palestinian peace talks.
"These are matters for Israelis to resolve," said U.S. envoy Dennis Ross during yet another regional shuttle to revive talks that have veered off track repeatedly since Netanyahu's election last May.
"That's the diplomat speaking," said a senior Western official. "The fact is if Bibi is fighting for his political life it can only be bad news for Washington's peacemaking."
Palestinians too, were wary of commenting on "Bibi" Netanyahu's domestic woes over his short-lived appointment of political crony Roni Bar-On as atttorney general.
After a three-month inquiry, police recommended in a 995-page report partially leaked on Wednesday that the state prosecution indict Netanyahu for fraud and breach of trust.
Netanyahu's lawyer and spokesmen dismissed the charges as baseless and talked of a political smear campaign.
The present attorney general is not bound to accept the police recommendations, which would leave Netanyahu unscathed legally.
The political and moral fallout, however, could be considerable.

"If they press charges that's the end of the government. No question," said a senior Likud source who asked not to be identified. "If they don't there will still be a period of instability. Whatever the legal outcome, politically and morally Netanyahu has already lost a great deal," the source said.
"Let's not talk about morality and this government," said Goodman, who has repeatedly lambasted Netanyahu for bad leadership.
"His problem will be with people like Sharon and Meridor who won't mind seeing him in trouble," Goodman said.

Netanyahu has made many enemies within Likud and the right-wing nationalist camp of his centre-right coalition government. These include the influential Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon and Finance Minister Dan Meridor.
Even if Netanyahu can quell dissent within his own party ranks the vital centrist component of his coalition could balk at being associated with an Israeli version of Nixon and Watergate.

Natan Sharansky's Russian-based Yisrael ba-Aliya party and Labour renegade Avigdor Kahalani's Third Way account for 11 of Netanyahu's 68 seats in the 120-member parliament. If they bolt the coalition, he would be forced in to an election or a unity government with the opposition Labour party.
Both Sharansky and Kahalani have frequently voiced concern since the corruption charges first broke in an Israel Channel One television report in January.
Police have not published the findings of their inquiry and Israeli media have offered only scant evidence of high-level government corruption.
The domestic press, however, has kept the spotlight on Netanyahu, claiming that the whole affair puts a question mark over his character and political leadership.
Supporters say Netanyahu's rise from nowhere through the ranks of Likud show he's a political heavy hitter.
But even his staunchest allies concede he is in for a rough bout.
"I predict a period of instability and embarrassment," a Likud official added.
